Apprehend

/ap-ri-HEND/ - rhymes with defend · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Apprehend means to seize or arrest someone.

Two off-duty constables apprehended the pickpocket in the theater lobby before the intermission crowd noticed a single missing watch.

Worked Example

The warrant sat unserved for a year until a hotel clerk recognized the forger's handwriting in the register; constables apprehended him that same evening at the boardinghouse card table, his winnings still stacked in front of him.

Apprehend is the official word for taking a suspect into custody — more formal than 'catch,' narrower than 'capture,' which can take soldiers, animals, or a chess piece. Police apprehend a suspect; nobody apprehends a runaway dog.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

arrest: Arrest is the plain legal word for taking someone into custody once charges attach — it is what the law does and what officers say. Apprehend does the same work in a more formal register: the word of reports and dispatches, and its object is always a suspect.

collar: Collar is the informal, almost gleeful word — an officer collars a thief in the act, hand on the scruff of his coat. Apprehend is its opposite in register: the same seizure of a suspect, but written up formally for the report, the dispatch, and the courtroom.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

release: to let someone out of custody

liberate: to set free, often with force or fanfare

Where it sits · how formal and lasting the custody is — detain → apprehend → incarcerate

detain vs. apprehend: To detain someone is to hold them briefly — an hour in a side room while papers are checked; detain stops short of apprehend, which is the formal seizure of a suspect.

incarcerate vs. apprehend: Incarcerate goes further than apprehend: an arrest begins custody, while incarceration is the long lock-and-key that a court may order afterward.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ap-

Prefix — ap-: to, toward

Root — prehend

Root — prehend: to seize, to grasp

Put it together

Put it together: Ap- (a form of ad-, 'to') + prehend (to seize) = to seize hold of. Latin prehendere gives English its grasping family — a monkey's prehensile tail, a firm grip on a subject — and apprehend is the law's version: taking hold of a suspect. English also lets the mind do the grasping, which is why apprehend can mean 'understand.'

Use the root in a new word: prehensile

Use the root in a new word: prehensile: A monkey's prehensile tail can seize a branch as surely as a hand.

Word Choice

formal / official

Apprehend belongs to reports and dispatches; in conversation, officers simply 'catch' or 'arrest' someone. One caution: apprehend has a second, bookish sense — to grasp with the mind, as in 'she apprehended the danger at once' — so let context show which grip you mean.
